thread.title: Jobless claims climb to 231,000 at end of 2018 amid government shutdown

author: Jeffry Bartash
title: Jobless claims climb to 231,000 at end of 2018 amid government shutdown
text:
Getty Images Jobless claims rose at the end of December. The numbers: The number of Americans who applied for unemployment benefits in the final week of 2018 rose to the highest level since Thanksgiving, an increase likely inflated by the partial government shutdown and the end of temporary staffing during the holiday season.
Initial jobless claims, a rough way to measure layoffs, climbed by 10,000 to a seasonally adjusted 231,000 in the seven days ended Dec. 29. Economists polled by MarketWatch had forecast a 218,000 reading.
New claims for the prior week were also revised up by 5,000 to 221,000.
What happened: Jobless claims often gyrate during the holiday season and into early January, making them less reliable as an economic indicator. Many Americans don’t file claims right away, government offices aren’t always open and lots of workers are let go from their temporary jobs after sales wind down.
A partial shutdown of the federal government may have also inflated claims, though a government official said it could not be determined if that were the case. New claims rose in Maryland but fell in Virginia, two states with a heavy concentration of federal employees.
The more stable monthly average of new claims fell by 500 to 218,750, marking the lowest level in a month and a half. And the number of raw claims — before the government adjusts for seasonal variations — was actually much lower compared to one year ago.
In other words, investors probably shouldn’t take the latest increase in claims as gospel.
The number of people already collecting unemployment benefits, meanwhile, rose by 32,000 to 1.74 million. These claims remain near a 45-year low, however.
Big picture: The economy is closing in on its 10th year of expansion, powered by the strongest labor market in almost two decades. The U.S. added more than 200,000 new jobs a month through the first 11 months of 2018 to push the unemployment rate down to a 49-year low of 3.7%.
On Friday, the government is expected to report that the economy added close to 200,000 new jobs in December, with the unemployment rate possibly falling another tick to 3.6%.
As long as that keeps up, the U.S. is sure to continue to avoid a recession. Wall Street is likely to watch initial claims closely early in the new year for signs of deterioration in the labor market that have so far been absent.

What they are saying? The “figures will remain choppy through the first five to six weeks of the year, although the underlying trend should remain low,” said chief economist Scott Brown of Raymond James.
Market reaction: The Dow Jones Industrial Average DJIA, -2.17% and S&P 500 SPX, -1.63% fell sharpy in Thursday trades after Apple AAPL, -8.92% said sales are likely to fall short of expectations.
The 10-year Treasury yield TMUBMUSD10Y, -1.34% slipped to 2.64%. Yields have tumbled from a seven-year high of 3.23% in October.
Jeffry Bartash Jeffry Bartash is a reporter for MarketWatch in Washington.
